speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the matter just came to my attention, and the minister to which I wish to address my question of privilege was absent from the House. So I beg Your Honour's indulgence that I might be permitted to proceed on this.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. 1 rise because of an inadvertent, misleading statement made in the House a few days ago. Before I begin, I should like to thank the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Miss MacDonald) for a letter which was delivered to my desk a few moments ago indicating that the government has at least gone part way toward the request I made last Wednesday.
My question related to a nuclear power plant close to the Canadian border at Sedro Woolley, Washington. Even before the accident at Three Mile Island, the people in my part of the country were extremely worried about this prospect.
I should like to address myself now to the question. My question last Wednesday, as reported at page 802 of Hansard, reads as follows;
-In view of the fact that a huge nuclear power plant is proposed for Sedro Woolley, in Washington's Skagit Valley, and since the site chosen is only 35 miles from population centres in British Columbia totalling almost one million people and should an accident ever take place massive environmental and evacuation problems would likely be encountered, what is the government's attitude toward the building of this nuclear power plant so close to our border? Is it one of official approval, disapproval, or indifference?
The reply I received from the Secretary of State for External Affairs reads as follows:
Mr. Speaker, this is a concern that has been expressed to me by many members on this side of the House as well as members in the opposition parties. While it is impossible for Canada to determine where the United States, or interests in the United States, will locate their nuclear power plants, nevertheless we have raised this subject with officials of the U.S. State Department.
I regard this as a reassuring reply. I and other members were left with the distinct impression that the phrase "we have raised this subject with officials of the U.S. State Department" meant that Canada had opposed the site at Sedro. That is precisely what the minister's answer implied, although perhaps unintentionally. One could hardly be blamed for assuming,
Privilege-Mr. Rose
because members on both sides of the House had expressed concern, that the minister was concerned too, that Canada had done more than merely raise the subject with the United States but in fact had declared its opposition to the location.
However, I have received a diplomatic letter, an aide memoire, which indicates precisely the opposite. Referring to page 3 of the aide memoire dated August 29 this year, it reads as follows:
Therefore, although the Government of Canada is not opposed in principle to the construction of a nuclear power station near the border, it wishes to be kept informed of project developments, particularly with respect to questions of public safety and environmental risk.
Regardless of what was said to me and other members of the House, the official policy of Canada is not to disapprove of new plants near our border. On the contrary, it is one of approval, or at the very least one of non-opposition.
In conclusion, when the minister rises to respond I hope she will report that Canada has now reversed its policy and will advise President Carter when he visits on Friday of this new change of heart.

However, he will know, having looked at the aide memoire to which he made reference-that is the aide memoire of August 29, and my letter to him of today following his letter to me of November 1-that we had told the United States government that we wanted to be fully informed about all aspects of this proposal which is very much in a preliminary state at the present time. We indicated that we want to be

November 6, 1979
Privilege-Mr. Rose
fully informed on all aspects of this proposal that relate to safety, particularly safety in regard to transboundary implications. The aide memoire states-and I think, sir, perhaps the hon. member should have read right through to the end of the aide-memoire:

Order, please. The House will realize, of course, that we have an area of perhaps disagreement between the two parties. Therefore, this does not fall within the ambit of a question of privilege.
I think I must take this occasion to say to the House that up to this point in this session I think 1 have been lenient in allowing members the opportunity to rise on questions of privilege, even though they essentially have been raising areas of disagreement with a minister. The difficulty in my continuing to do so is clearly that whenever this takes place, the member having put one side of the question it is only appropriate, of course, that the minister have an opportunity to respond.
1 do not single out this particular case today as there have been a number of them, but the end result is that the member who raises such a disagreement with a minister is in effect extending the question period and getting an additional go-around which every member would like to enjoy.
If I am to be generous in this regard, and then allow equal time for a minister to respond in each case, what I will in fact be doing out of this generosity is inviting members to do more than they can accomplish in question period by attempting to extend the question period through some procedural point after the question period is over. That would be patently unfair and would also take up a great deal of debating time as, for example, today when there is a motion which, of course, the House is anxious to debate.
I do not distinguish this case from any others that have taken place. 1 do not take a more severe view of this case than of any other case. I simply say to the House that I will have to take a little harder line in respect of these questions, and if members rise to their feet and indicate at the outset a matter

not of significance immediately but rather one of disagreement, I will probably have to stop them before they develop the point for too long and, therefore, before it would be only fair to invite a minister to respond.

The second important policy that our government had to establish in the matter of petroleum was that of pricing, Mr. Speaker. 1 plead with this government, which has managed to change its mind on so many issues, to come back to Liberal policies in this regard.

What does the government see as its policy? Apparently it is scrapping the existing price agreement and is telling us that it is going to move toward international prices. What will this mean, Mr. Speaker? If international prices were to come very soon, they would mean about $400 per year more for home heating oil and $250 per year more for the average automobile driver. They would mean loss of jobs to industry. They would mean, Mr. Speaker, that the economy, which has already been subjected to the shock of record high interest rates, would be subjected to the double shock of heating oil and petroleum prices which cannot be accepted and assimilated by the economy at this time.

First of all, I want to remind the House that our policy was set out quite clearly in the "Energy Strategy for Canada" published in the early months of 1976. I should like to read from page 127 on which the following passage appears:
We must continue the process that began in April of 1974, of phasing the price of domestic oil towards international levels. Canada does not necessarily have to go to international prices. Because we have domestic resources to develop, we have a degree of independence from the oil-exporting cartel that many countries do not enjoy and that is to our advantage.
Our policy was to have prices at a level where resources could be found, where they could be developed and delivered. That does not mean any price which could be established by a cartel acting on international markets in a way which would be deemed illegal if it so acted in Canada. There is no reason why we would have to follow world prices, no matter what level they went to.

November 6, 1979
Severe Economic Hardship
We agreed when we reached various understandings with the government of Alberta, the government of Saskatchewan and with other provinces that prices could not remain at the levels that had prevailed before 1972. We agreed that there had to be some increase if exploration and development were to continue in Canada. But we never did agree, we do not agree now and the country does not agree, with a policy that says that no matter what this cartel decides Canadians who have energy resources of their own will have to go to those cartel prices. We do not agree to that on oil and we did not agree on other natural resources.
I just remind this House of a policy announced in April 1969 by the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Pepin), who was then minister of industry trade and commerce, that copper prices would be sold in Canada at prices below the London copper exchange prices, because those London prices were established in a way which was not guided by the free law of supply and demand but by action on that market which was not fair, free and unfettered. We did that on copper, we did that on oil, and what is more, Mr. Speaker, we did it with the agreement of the Premier of Alberta. We did it at a time when many provinces wanted to see no increase at all.
We stated then and we state now that our policy is not to increase prices indefinitely. We hear from Syncrude that the price of extracting a barrel of oil from the tar sands is now estimated at between $15 and $20. Our experts think that it is closer to $14 or $15 a barrel. Never mind, even taking Syncrude's figures, surely there is no need to go to $25, $35 or $50 a barrel.

I just want to conclude on this very important subject.

Canada is now up against tremendous problems. We may be on the brink of a recession the like of which Canadians have not seen in several decades. We know what threat that represents not only to industry, and the resulting loss of jobs, but especially what danger there is that oil prices be fixed by an international cartel on the backs of the people, which would make heating their houses more costly and would also make the cost of driving their cars go up.
We know indeed that it is not easy to run a country these days. We know that there is inflation in the world, that there is unemployment, but we say to the government, Mr. Speaker, that it is precisely in such circumstances that governments have a crucial and fundamental role to play. We cannot afford to have a government which remains in the background and watches the provinces fighting together. We cannot afford to have a government which thinks that top performance for a government is to let things go. What have we witnessed over the last six months? We have seen a government which is trying to apply a maxim whose author and main proponent is Jim Gillies, always the same, the senior adviser to the Prime Minister, who said:

On the supply of essential petroleum supplies, we have a government which dismantles Petro-Canada and lets the multinationals decide on supply to Canada. Severe Economic Hardship
says we will let the United States decide and we will follow their policy, no matter how high it goes.
We have a government which has abdicated the role of government. We have a government which again yesterday was giving us as the greatest examples of being able to bring harmony to federal-provincial relations and to put a new face on federalism, a government that had managed to rid itself of Loto Canada and a government which had managed to rid itself of its jurisdiction over the offshore resources. Yet last Friday, the hon. member for Outremont (Mr. Lalonde) and myself tried four times to get the Prime Minister to say that his ministers from Quebec would campaign for the "No" option. Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to conclude by saying that if the Prime Minister honestly believes that he is going to win Quebeckers by offering them Loto Canada and telling them that his government is prepared to change the status quo, without specifying how he is going to do that, then this government and its Prime Minister do not know Quebeckers very well because they want a government that stands on its own two feet. Mr. Speaker, we have just heard why the phrase which was used by my colleague, the hon. member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. Rose), was so accurate. The Liberal party is clearly a party not in opposition but in exile. It lost its raison d'etre when it was in government and it has not found its purpose for itself now that it is in opposition.
I rise to support the motion-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext:
Our friends in exile laugh. 1 will see if they are laughing in a minute. We support the motion. We support the words but not necessarily the motives behind them. I can tell the House that.
In campaigning for the May 22 election, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) campaigned on the economy. Before May 22 he said he was concerned about the devastating effects that interest rates were having on the people of Canada. He said they were causing an increase in the cost of living, producing more unemployment and contributing to a lower rate of economic growth.
The Prime Minister was right before May 22; high interest rates do all of those things. My party says that what they did before May 22 they have continued to do since. We have not been able to understand the scintillating logic behind the present government's position. Before the election the Prime Minister was saying that if you have a high interest rate policy, it will produce those bad things. He turned out to be right, but what is his conclusion? His answer was to reproduce the policy which caused all the bad things.
We know that high interest rates are bad for Canadians. We further know that they are unnecessary. I spent the last two days in western Canada. For the benefit of the Prime Minister and his government I want to give some concrete examples from western Canada of the results of his high interest rate policy. First in terms of the cost of living-and this should interest the Prime Minister, coming as he does from Alberta- the cost of living has its effect on every aspect of the economy, whether we are talking about bicycles, food, cars, or any commodity. High interest rates are devastating because they are all passed on to the consumer.
I was watching the news in Saskatchewan two days ago and there was an item coming from Calgary. It said that as a result of the increase in interest rates, not before May 22, not even in the first two months of the summer, but simply as a result of the increases in interest rates which have occurred in the last two months, the monthly carrying charge of a typical home in Calgary had gone up by $146 a month, which means that the average person in that city can no longer buy a home. The average Canadian living in Calgary who is reasonably prosper-

ous can no longer buy a home as a direct result of this government's high interest rate policy. Another statistic which came out during the same program was that housing sales had dropped 22 per cent this year in the city of Calgary because of the escalation of prices, principally due to rising interest rates.
On the same visit to the west I spoke to farmers in Saskatchewan, I spoke to them in Prince Albert, I had a meeting in a small community by the name of Weldon and the farmers there are typical. A typical loan for a farmer, even if he is prosperous, can be up to $15,000 a year when the farmer has to borrow to purchase fertilizer and chemicals to run his operation on a continuing basis. Interest rate increases on $15,000 a year of the kind that have been taking place are devastating for the farmers of western Canada and elsewhere.
I had one moving experience with a man I would guess to be in his mid-sixties who has a farm in Saskatchewan. This man told me that up until last week his son had intended to buy a farm; he had planned to follow the family tradition of farming but with the last interest rate increase that young man concluded he could not afford to carry on the family tradition of farming. He could not afford to buy a farm. That is the fault of the Conservative government and no one else. There are literally in every part of this country examples of this kind that could be passed on, concrete, living examples of the effects of a high interest rate policy in terms of cost. But also they count very seriously and directly in terms of the impact on jobs, in terms of opportunities for Canadian men and women who want to work.
Today in the question period one of our members from British Columbia drew attention in the House to a decision of the largest manufacturer of plywood in that province, Weld-wood of Canada Limited, to lay off a minimum of 600 employees. Why? Because of the decline in the housing market. If I had time I could quote a number of statements coming from both management and union in that company in the last 24 hours saying there is one reason and one reason only that housing is running down in British Columbia and across this land. Again it is because of the high interest rate policy of this government. The point I am making is that it is jobs that are affected in this case, not just the cost of living.
I particularly want to draw attention to small businessmen. Large companies in the main generate their own capital but small firms throughout the land do have to go to the banks or the credit unions or the caisses populaires. The problem facing small business is that in today's circumstances not only are they unable to obtain at reasonable rates the capital needed for expansion, but in some cases they are obliged to shut down completely and lay off Canadian workers. The point I am making, and it has been made by many members in my party not only since the election but before, is that a high interest rate policy, whether it comes from the Liberals or from the Tories, is equally bad for the country in its effect upon job creation and the cost of living.
1 want in particular to pay tribute to the argument that was put by my hon. friend from Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae) to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic
November 6, 1979

Affairs-and it was not in any way answered-that not only are high interest rates damaging to the people of Canada, but they are unnecessary. 1 do not have the time to repeat the argument but I ask the Prime Minister, if he does not accept the argument coming from the New Democratic Party, to read the columns by Mr. Don. McGillivray, an independent economist, a fair-minded man who had reached the same conclusion. Will he read a report which was published, I understand, in the last 24 hours by two Toronto economists, Roger Donna and Doug Peters, who have done a critique of the Bank of Canada's policies over the past five years and, related to that, a critique, therefore, of the Liberal party and the Conservative party who have been responsible for the Bank of Canada policy. They drew the conclusion that not only are the effects of high interest rates harmful to our people in the short run; they are economically unnecessary and are very bad indeed for the long-range growth of this country. I say on behalf of my colleagues, the Prime Minister was right when he criticized high interest rates before May 22. The same arguments hold today and it is about time he lived up to his promise to bring them down.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext:
1 want to turn now to oil pricing. The position of my party has been again consistent on this issue. We have said that at this time it is wrong, given the state of the Canadian economy, to move upward to world prices. We think that is a serious mistake both because of its effects on the inflationary side of the ledger and on the job creation side. It is very negative at this time to move in that direction. We have pointed out that other countries which are oil producers-Venezuela, Mexico, Saudi Arabia-manage to produce oil and gas for their own people at prices lower than they charge to the world community because they sensibly understand that with lower prices you help your domestic industry, you help your consumers. We believe our resources should be used for that kind of benefit here.
In this context we urged the government as recently as last week to establish what we have called a commission on oil prices and profits, not one which would arbitrarily roll back every proposed increase but one which would operate with some intellectual and economic sophistication, which would look at price increases and, where they are unjustified, as in the case of multinational corporations which have taken, as even President Carter in the United States recognizes, rip-off profits, would have the authority to order rollbacks.
Yes, we have said that and we believe it. We have also said such a commission should come before the government and make serious recommendations for price increases, if and when necessary, to produce investment, to get new sources of energy at terms we think reasonable and compatible with the Canadian national interest and not compatible simply with the interests of the multinational corporations. We stand by this argument today.
1 say to the Prime Minister in this context that if ever there was a time for the relevance of Petro-Canada, it surely is when
Severe Economic Hardship
we are talking about oil prices. 1 say this in terms of the need for more competition at the retail outlets in Atlantic Canada where Irving and Imperial Oil own 60 per cent of the retail outlets, but more particularly I say it, Mr. Speaker, with reference to the negotiations taking place for the development of our tar sands, the oil sands project which is now being discussed, as well as others. Shell wants up to 20 per cent guaranteed profit for that development.
My party says that we have PetroCan which has acquired expertise in the Syncrude project and which has the technical know-how. PetroCan can get the equipment and it should be doing the job for the people of Canada without earning a profit in that project.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext: So we are saying that all the oil price increases which the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Hnatyshyn) and the Prime Minister like to use to justify funds for resource development in the north are simply unjustified, because we have a Crown corporation that can do that job for the people of Canada at cost.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext: Next I come to the very important matter of heating oil shortages. This is a real problem which cannot be ignored, and it is not something that is in the future. The National Energy Board said on the weekend that it would be rash to predict with certainty that Canadians will be free of oil supply problems this winter. That is a warning and it is not new now. We have been arguing a workable solution to this for a couple of years. On the one hand we have said that the National Energy Board should never be signing carte blanche authorizations for the export of home heating gas or oil months in advance. In every kind of export contract that is negotiated there should be a qualifying clause which says that if a shortage should emerge in Canada, oil and gas will have to stay to meet Canadian needs.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext:
The second point I make in that regard is that here again we have a clear argument for Petro-Canada. Just a couple of weeks ago we had an amendment to the Liberal motion which said that Petro-Canada should become the exclusive importer of offshore oil, and one of the reasons we made that argument-again, I repeat, not just currently but for some time-is that we saw what happened last winter in the province of Quebec when the Exxon Corporation and its subsidiary here in Canada, Imperial Oil, was detouring supplies headed for this country. We have seen the multinationals cut off the independent dealers when it suited their purposes, and we have said that Petro-Canada should become the exclusive importer of oil so we will not be held up to blackmail by the multinational corporations. On this particular point I underscore the reality that when we had that motion before us,

November 6, 1979
Severe Economic Hardship
not only did the government vote against it and the Social Credit party vote against it, but the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Trudeau) and his party voted against it; and now they are expressing concern here.
For all these reasons, we will certainly support the motion that is before us today. The government has not come through at all in terms of its pledges to deal with the Canadian economy. Today I have emphasized in particular the question of interest rates. Second, the government has produced no energy policy at all except that dictated by Peter Lougheed on the one hand, and the multinationals on the other.
Having said that about the government, I now want to turn briefly to the Liberal party. We have seen a presentation today coming from what has become the most cynical political party in Canadian history without doubt.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext: They are utterly shameless about the way they have reversed themselves overnight, not only on matters in general but, as 1 shall indicate, on virtually every aspect of the motion they presented to the House today, and they do it shamelessly. The reality of the Liberal party at this point in its history is that it is functioning without either intellectual substance or a moral core. Its sole concern has become the pursuit of power. That is the raison d'etre of the Liberal party as it exists today.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext: It takes one to know one.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext: The present Leader of the Opposition-and I use the words with some care because that is the title-has said that the Liberals in Canada have become a party of the radical centre.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext: Right on.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext: A Liberal says "right on". I would suggest that a more accurate description is that they have become the party of the cynical centre or, more precisely, the party of the dead centre.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext:
In every aspect of this motion we can see cynicism at work in the Liberal party. It was the Liberals who began, in the summer of 1978, the current economic philosophy that has been implemented by their friends who now constitute the Government of Canada. It was the Liberals who introduced UIC changes which brought in the cutbacks in the summer of 1978. It was the Liberals who first promised to privatize a number of Crown corporations and who produced, not one, not two, not three but seven increases in interest rates between January 1 of 1978 and the time when the new government was elected. Seven increases in interest rates! Now they have the nerve to get up hypocritically and attack the government for carrying on their good Liberal tradition. I ask you, Mr. Speaker.

Similarly, the Leader of the Opposition has spoken with care about the problem of heating oil shortages. When shortages appeared last winter, the Liberals, who were then in government, responded in their typically direct, forthright and forceful way: they had an investigation. That was it. Then on the weekend-this weekend-when the NEB drew the attention of the people of Canada to the fact that we may have some shortages, they said the shortages were not due just to the present government permitting exports to take place of this important commodity but it was the previous Liberal government which last winter went on permitting NEB to negotiate export contracts for home heating oil that are now putting our people in jeopardy this winter. The Liberals were doing it themselves.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext: Morals of an alley cat.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext:
As to the question of oil pricing-Mr. Speaker, I see my time is just about up. I wonder if I could extend my comments for a few moments, if the House would courteously grant me that time to wind up my remarks quickly.
On the question of oil pricing about which the Liberals are so concerned today, I should like to quote the former minister of energy, mines and resources who, not five or six years ago but on November 30, said:
Our policy has been and still is, to move crude oil prices at the well head toward world levels.
The motion calls our attention to changes which took place in terms of interprovincial agreements; that is of the then Liberal government and the provinces. I would remind the Leader of the Opposition that it was the present official opposition which, when they were in government last winter, changed the existing agreement. I believe the best way to describe the situation at this time is to say that it is tight but under control. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Hnatyshyn) as well as the chairman of the National Energy Board have been constantly monitoring the situation for weeks and months.
We did not wait until we had a crisis this winter to act, and concrete steps have been taken to deal with any major problem that could occur in coming months. That is why the volume of our exports of crude oil abroad have been reduced considerably, in fact nearly eliminated so as to fully meet the demand by Canadian refiners. With the approval of the government, the National Energy Board is allowed to swap Canadian western crude for additional supplies of foreign oil to eastern Canada. The last item in the Leader of the Opposition's motion concerns interest rates. No one in this House, and 1 am sure no Canadian, likes high interest rates. We all want them lowered and this government is determined that they be lowered, not by instant magic, because there is no magic, but by taking the tough decisions now that are essential if we are going to restore the Canadian economy to the kind of strength that will allow more moderate rates of interest in the future. That, sir, is our medium-term goal and we are dedicated to it.
However, the issue in this motion is the short term- whether the government had any immediate alternative but to accept the advice of the governor of the Bank of Canada and, indeed, what the consequences following an alternative course might have been. The hard reality is that the economic circumstances we inherited from the old government left us with no short-term alternative. In fact, on becoming the government it became apparent to us that the mess was even worse than we suspected and that our immediate options were even more limited than we thought they were. We knew that we were inheriting a budgetary deficit of $11 billion, the largest in Canadian history. We knew that we were stuck with a balance of payments deficit of some $7 billion, the worst per capita deficit in international dealings of any western nation.
But let me tell the House a few of the facts we found out only after we became the Government of Canada. First,

because of the previous government's commitment to secrecy, we did not know that the trend in government finances was exactly opposite to what Canadians had been told by the old government. We found that long-range forecasts, which we made public for the first time, showed the federal deficit increasing to $14 billion by 1983 and the public debt actually growing dramatically again with the next five years.
Secondly, we had been told by the former minister of finance, as recently as his last budget, that the Canadian economy was entering into a period of, to use his words, "sustained expansion". What we found in fact was an economy here and in the United States sliding toward a recession, not moving toward sustained expansion.
The third thing we found was that the accounts of Canada, as presented by the old government, simply did not represent the true financial position of the country. In the Accounts of Canada Adjustments Act, the previous government proposed to write off some $3.5 billion in dubious assets, an action which might not affect cash requirements but which certainly had an impact on the country's net debt and debt servicing costs. Similarly, we found Crown corporation borrowings of as much as $1.5 billion which were not entered in the accounts, even though they were a contingent liability of the government. We found a number of capital projects with costs virtually out of control, from the Prince Rupert grain dryer, where costs had multiplied five times, to the Mirabel Airport losing $1 million a week and requiring expenditures of hundreds of millions of dollars before it could even achieve solvency.

Mr. Speaker, faced with this legacy, no responsible government had any other alternative but to accept rising interest rates. Our government made a difficult but responsible choice. Let me also tell you the other solution we could have adopted. The Liberals as well as the New Democrats have hinted to the Canadian public, without ever making their position clear, that there was an obvious way out, which as Canadians should know, which had the full support of the opposition, namely, to reject the advice of the governor of the Bank of Canada.
Such a decision would have had dire consequences. The governor might have felt he had to resign, as the government's decision would amount to a lack of confidence. Given the present economic situation, such a resignation might have provoked a wind of panic on the Canadian stock exchange and dealt a hard blow to Canadian currency. Even without the Governor's resignation, our dollar would have been affected by our $7 billion trade deficit, followed by a drastic depreciation of our dollar and serious inflationary consequences for our country.
Such was, Mr. Speaker, the short-term choice the government had to make. 1 hope the representatives of the two parties opposite will have the courage to rise before this debate is over and tell this House and the Canadian people that it was the option they supported.

The vote under no circumstances, may I say, can be taken to pass out of existence a political party, nor can it be taken to render as independent members the group which has been recognized as a party and which has, in fact, been seated together as a political party. The Social Credit Party of Canada exists as a political party and the five members exist as members of that party under their leader.
Faced with the decision by the House on the one hand, which was, in my opinion, an expression of what the entitlement of that group then becomes, the House decided at that time that that group, as a political party in the House, was not entitled to membership automatically on the striking committee. The House is entitled to make those expressions because the House has to decide whether a party of five members is entitled to the same things as a party of 26 members or a party of 112 members. Those are decisions that the House has to make. The House, in my opinion, made a declaration to that effect on that day, and I have said so several times. I have no intention of retreating from that position.
On the other hand, it seems to me that the responsibility of the Chair and the responsibility of the House of Commons is to protect whatever rights minorities do enjoy and, therefore, it seems to me that I must conclude what it is that the members of the Social Credit party are entitled to. For example, as I have said, participation in the question period is their right, the same as any other group of five members. It is not difficult to calculate mathematically what five members are entitled to as a proportion of the 26 members and a proportion in terms of the 112 members that sit opposite them. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have before us this afternoon a non-confidence motion put forward by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Trudeau). The motion reads as follows, and I quote:
That this House has no confidence in the government because it will cause severe economic hardship for the Canadian people this winter: first, through its neglect of the grave possibility of shortages in heating fuel; second, through its failure to support existing intergovernmental agreements on oil pricing and supply; third, through its inability to conclude agreements preventing immoderate price increases in the future; and, fourth, through its acceptance of record high interest rates.
Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to point out that making up one's mind on such a motion is a very difficult and delicate task. Canadians who are now listening to us must also be in this same predicament for if such a motion were to be accepted, this non-confidence motion against the new government would be tantamount to a confidence motion for the previous government.
Since coming to this House, 1 have heard hon. members from the opposition question the government. They ask the same questions the new government members were asking when they were the opposition. And I have heard government members, the new Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) for instance, give the same answers as the previous government did when

they were in power. 1 see the Prime Minister shaking his head. If he would read his statements and compare them with those made by the former prime minister, he would have to agree on this.
I paid close attention today to the speech delivered by the mover of the motion, and to the answer given by the Prime Minister, after listening of course to the remarks made by my colleague, the Leader of the New Democratic party (Mr. Broad bent).
The former prime minister said the new prime minister was an irresponsible leader, that he was incapable of finding solutions to our economic and energy problems. On the other hand, the new prime minister suggested that the former prime minister, when in government, was totally incapable of solving the economic problems and bringing true solutions to any of the areas of concern to Canadians. In other words, they accused each other and Mr. Speaker, I am reluctant to use these terms, because they are hardly parliamentary, they accused each other of being incompetent, so to speak. Seriously, Mr. Speaker, I am wondering whether both were not right to some extent. The Canadian people chose to elect a new government on May 22, and why? Because things were not working any more, and the previous government's deficits had become unacceptable. I heard the former Prime Minister suggest earlier before the House that the high cost of energy will amount to about $300 per capita, and this seems inevitable.
But he did not mention that in the last three years, budgetary deficits have put a yearly $500 debt on the back of every Canadian. The former prime minister did not mention that. And yet, it is a fact, because every year Parliament has to vote huge amounts in order to pay the interest on such a fantastic debt that long-term borrowings are now needed to make up the yearly budgetary deficits.
Mr. Speaker, how can we believe that the former prime minister, the sponsor of this motion, is sincere when he or his group does not seem any more able today than they were six months ago to settle our problems? That is why I would like to come back to the motion which is in four parts. First, it mentions the grave possibility of shortages in heating fuel. I feel this first part of the motion is extremely important. The second part deals with agreements to prevent price increases. I must say that to prevent an agreement on price increases in this inflationary period shows a very partisan attitude, because the present system, that no one on either side of the House seems willing to change, should be really improved so as to bring about the same results on both sides. So I really wonder if the second part of the motion can be called anything but partisan.
As concerns the third part according to which the government does not support intergovernmental agreements and
November 6, 1979

which refers to future negotiations, I think that only a prophet could predict the future. That is why I find somewhat ridiculous the third part of the motion. The fourth refers to interest rates, and 1 contend, Mr. Speaker, that it is completely irrational.
I had the opportunity, like my colleagues from various political parties, to question the governor of the Bank of Canada when he appeared before the parliamentary Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, and I asked him personally if he always had to follow the lead of the Federal Reserve Board in increasing interest rates and if he had to pursue the policy of the previous government because, as loyal knaves, they faithfully repeated, as if they had been tape-recorded, the decisions of the Federal Reserve Board. They have followed exactly the same policies. Neither government has proposed any short, medium or long-term solutions. So, when the former government speaks about Quebec when it has absolutely nothing to propose, I say it is wasting the time of the House.
As reported in Hansard, the governor of the Bank of Canada said that he had practically no room to manoeuvre and no authority, when he implied that the huge budgetary deficits of the government, the huge deficits of the balance of payments do not leave him any room to manoeuvre, and in order to save the dollar or maintain its value, he has to follow the instructions of the Federal Reserve Board.
When such an important man, a man who holds the high office of governor of the Bank of Canada, is reduced to saying such things, there is something wrong. If he could, he would say that had we had governments able to govern, able to make decisions in the interest of all Canadians, he would not find himself in such a ridiculous situation.
Obviously, a motion of non-confidence like the one before us today is exactly the kind of motion designed to make people believe that after four months of reflection and frustration in the opposition, some already have answers to our problems. This is an attempt to fool the people of Canada and to mislead them by throwing a red herring across the path so as to divert everybody's attention from 15 years of negligence and administrative irresponsibility.
Mr. Speaker, when we consider that the sum total of these deficits represents almost 6 per cent of the gross national product and consequently erodes-

Some hon. members are annoyed. It always hurts to be told the facts. However, since my arrival in this House, I have always had the courtesy to listen without ever interrupting, and I ask to be treated with the same courtesy.
Severe Economic Hardship
When one considers that the total of these two deficits represents close to 6 per cent of the GNP and consequently erodes nearly 25 per cent of the present and future savings of Canadians, it is time to start asking ourselves some serious questions. To blame this government when you are the ones mainly responsible is somewhat ridiculous, but still not surprising coming from those who brought about the present situation.
The infringement of civil liberties-we shall have some other chance of bringing this up. The encroachment upon provincial rights-we shall have the chance of discussing this much further during the forthcoming few weeks or months, also the basic violation of the right to economic progress of the Canadian people throughout the country. The third point is absolute nonsense: blaming the government for failing to bring about agreements preventing price increases is pure fantasy. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, the situation inherited from the previous government amounts to a complete surrender to foreign capitals. We have become a sort of subsidiary for foreign financial interests and the Canadian monetary policy no longer originates in Canada. We have no such policy. It is based solely on the decisions of others, and both the present and the previous governments have admitted to what extent the situation has deteriorated and the new government seems to realize the facts.
Mr. Speaker, this abdication before foreign capitals is reflected by the constant increases in our exports of raw materials. We export our raw materials and import finished products. We have only to look at our trade balance to realize this. This complete abdication is reflected by the naive will to believe that pious wishes can replace political leadership. When 1 say "pious wishes" I am referring to both the new government and the former government because they are no longer responsible for the management of the nation's business.
This surrender is reflected in the fact that the financial situation which the present government is facing is such that they must borrow to pay the interest on the debt, to improve our balance of payments and to attract international capital, which makes us even more dependent on foreign finance and in the long term only increases the deficit of the balance of payments.
Because of the legacy of the previous government whose basic misunderstanding of business structures becomes more obvious every day, the Leader of the Opposition is stating in his motion:
__its inability to conclude agreements preventing immoderate price increases in
the future;
In the first place, agreements on price increases, as far as I know, are prohibited; I venture to say that the Leader of the Opposition has made a mistake. Second, future prices-there again is the height of ridicule. Through what, where, when and

November 6, 1979
Severe Economic Hardship
how was the future revealed to the Leader of the Opposition? After all, these people should be more serious.
Mr. Speaker, 1 could dwell at length on our economic situation, on the way the country has been managed during the 15 or 16 years of Liberal rule, on the way this wavering government seems unable to make decisions and depends on foreign powers and decisions made outside Canada.
Mr. Speaker, 1 should like to come back to an important matter, a fundamental one, energy. That is why when we learned about the motion to be introduced by the Liberal party, we wanted to make a positive effort. Instead of criticizing the government, we wanted to ask them to assume their responsibilities. I therefore took upon myself to write a letter to the Prime Minister in which I stressed two points, letting him know that it was extremely important that his government should announce immediately to the Canadian people the measures he had taken or intended to take and the guarantees he could give to prevent any risk of shortages, and avoid the panic that could result in unreasonable price increases.
Second, we said to the government, through the Prime Minister, that it was also extremely important that every step be taken to protect quotas and make sure they were available to independent distributors. Just today the Prime Minister sent us a very lengthy letter of four pages in which he provides particulars following our request which we considered to be constructive. We asked for some explanations and since verba volant, scripta manent, the Prime Minister is bound by the comments he made in his letter. The Prime Minister answered that the short-term situation-unfortunately 1 will not have enough time, because the Standing Orders will not allow me to read the entire letter.

The short-term situation as we found it last June was also far from satisfactory. Inventories had been seriously depleted and there was considerable uncertainty about the adequacy of gasoline supply for the summer and heating oil for the winter.
The government acted promptly to improve the situation and to secure equitable treatment for the independent sector of the business. Thus:
1.	With the co-operation of the government of Alberta and its agencies, production of crude oil in western Canada has been brought to maximum levels in recent months.
2.	Exports of our valuable light crude oil were reduced from 55,000 barrels a day in September to 14,000 barrels a day in October and virtually eliminated in November in order to make this oil available to Canadian refiners.
3.	With the government's approval, the National Energy Board has continued to allow the exchange of western Canadian oil for additional supplies of overseas oil to eastern Canada. The Energy Board recently approved exchanges totalling some 2.5 million barrels, virtually all of which are for the account of refiners in the province of Quebec.
4.	The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has authorized the payment of special import compensation in the amount of $745,000 to enable a Quebec refiner to import a badly-needed cargo of crude oil despite an unexpected increase in its price.
5.	On July 13 the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources released a report of an inquiry into problems which distributors, particularly in Quebec had faced last winter. The recommendations of the inquiry are being vigorously pursued.

Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. I appreciate your great wisdom.
I would like to ask the right hon. Prime Minister to give us more information regarding independent distributors. The words procedure and recommendations have been mentioned. We are not aware of these recommendations. We would like to get more detailed and precise information. When the Prime Minister talks about procedure, we would like to know which ones have been followed to ensure that all necessary measures have been taken so that people will not suffer any hardships arising from this situation. The Prime Minister also informed us that a telex had been sent to the refineries. I would ask him to provide us with a copy of this message, to table it so that we know where we stand. We would also like to know whether the refineries and other companies have to submit regular reports to the National Energy Board in order to enable the latter to monitor the situation closely and regularly and also to prevent the development of a crisis situation, such as the one we now risk facing. Everyone knows of course that energy is at present an extremely important issue.
I would therefore ask the Prime Minister to give us this information before six o'clock if possible because we want to do a serious job. We are not in this House to play games. We want to go beyond words because even if we are bound by the rules to take a colleague's words, we still want to check the mechanisms, we want to be sure, at some point, of everything the government has done in that area. We want to be informed, and I would ask the Prime Minister to address his letter correctly, and I think he knows what I mean.

speechtext: Thank God for that.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext:
If you want my picture, Mr. Speaker, you are welcome to it. I do not care.
I want to say a few words on this motion of non-confidence. First, 1 should like to start by speaking about the purpose of the non-confidence motion. We have heard certain allusions to the motives for this non-confidence motion today. The Prime Minister simply said it was a ritual. If that was a ritual, then he has gone to an awful lot of effort to make a deal on that ritual.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext:
I think, Mr. Speaker, it is far more than a ritual. I would also say that the kind of vitriolic and poisonous

words which we heard from the Leader of the NDP (Mr. Broadbent), again challenging the reasons for our motion, only shows a man who is so frustrated by his own unrequited desire for power that he really should be challenged as to whose ethics are worse, and whether he is prepared to support a motion from members whose motives he does not accept. If the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie), who is a theologian of great standing, according to his own description, were here, he would find that the ethic as to whether the NDP can so willingly support a motion put forward by a party which they find so reprehensible is questionable. Perhaps it is because they are so used to looking at their own image.
The real point at issue is the purpose of a non-confidence motion. This is a serious motion-no one is treating it lightly or treating it with the kind of frivolity that hon. members opposite seem to have shown. We take the position that there is one basic fact that perhaps hon. members opposite tend to forget, that is, that they are a minority government. They neither command a majority of members in this House nor do they command a majority of votes in the country. As a minority government, they have the direct obligation and responsibility to listen to the majority. They have not been listening to the majority since this Parliament opened.
Today, we heard the Prime Minister express to the member of Parliament for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), I think, that he does not even want to listen to members of Parliament any more-he can rule by divine democracy, he can do it directly himself. But the point about minority government is that it must rest upon the confidence of the House, and the confidence of the House is held by the majority of members who are not sitting on that side. They are not Progressive Conservatives. We on this side represent far more of the population of Canada than members of the government.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext: With all the brave protestation about speaking for the people of Canada and listening to Parliament, it is about time the government started to listen. If the government were listening, it would hear the people saying that they are tired of interest rates over 15 per cent or 16 per cent and their businesses going broke. They are tired of not being able to buy houses, even though the promises are there. They are tired of having a national government being pushed around by provincial premiers. They are tired of living in the jeopardy of accelerating energy prices with no commitment to any form of support or cushion for those prices. A lot of people are tired of the government acting in a fashion which indicates that it is not prepared to listen to the majority of Canadians.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext:
The point of bringing in this non-confidence motion is very much like the old story which is told in western Canada. A farmer was seen hitting a donkey over the head with a two-by-four; he was asked why and he said, "To get its attention". We have brought in this motion to get the attention
November 6, 1979

of the government, so that it will start listening to what Canadians have to say. That is the purpose of the motion, not the cynical motives contributed by the hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party nor the rituals described by the Prime Minister. We are talking about a very serious initiative. It is one instrument available to an opposition party to provide a message to the government, a message which is particularly significant for a government in a minority position. It is about time the government began remembering that fact every day; we will keep reminding it.
The reasons are clear. Since Parliament has opened we have had direct denial and contradictions of the commitments, promises, and proposals put forward by members of the Progressive Conservative Party in the election campaign. They have not been prepared to live up, by their actions, to the words they expressed at that time. It is about time their actions began to lie closer to the truth, to what they believe.
We talk about interest rates. We recognize that this is not an easy problem. We do not have a simplistic, socialistic solution like the sparrows in the corner who twitter away. There is no magic answer to the problem. There is an economic time bomb on the international monetary scene. We recognize that the Bank of Canada and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) must be careful and cautious about the rates charged. Also we realize full well that they must protect the dollar. But they have an obligation to protect Canadians as well, and to ensure that the small businessman who spoke to me in my riding on Saturday has protection. That gentleman had a line of credit of $250,000. He said, "I can last two months and then I go under because I have no protection; 1 have no satisfaction and no way of getting any assistance. The government should be listening to that kind of person.
We have been trying to say, during question period and meetings of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, that if there is a requirement to raise interest rates, there is an equal requirement to help those people who are hurt by those interest rate increases. There is an equal requirement to ask a question which I do not think has been asked: do the rates have to go as high as they have? An hon. member from Thunder Bay, gave the Minister of Finance clear documentation showing that the spread between the nominal rate and the real rate has been growing larger over the last three months, not smaller, and therefore can justify a somewhat lower interest rate. But the Minister of Finance is so busy being a down-east version of Johnny Carson that he cannot concentrate long enough to decide what economic and fiscal policies he is prepared to introduce.
We listened with great interest to the declarations of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Crombie). In a provocative and sentimental statement the minister said, "I am concerned about the people in need." I believe that minister is concerned about the people in need, but the Minister of Finance is not because he is prepared to put $575 million into the budget this year to pay for a mortgage credit plan which has no economic use and is not going to the people in need. Is that good economics? Also I listened to the minister of housing
Severe Economic Hardship
who I think is a sincere, honest, forthright minister. On Thursday in committee he said, "Yes, there are real problems in the housing market". He indicated that people are defaulting on their mortgages, housing starts are going down, and the housing market will be in chaos.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext: They are up this month.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext:
The hon. member opposite does not know much about housing. By the first month in 1980 housing starts in the country will be down 30 per cent. That information comes from every industrial spokesman. The minister of housing said that he knew there was a problem, but he had no fiscal room; he had no money to spend. Why is the Minister of Finance laying $575 million on the table for a program which will not provide additional home ownership opportunities? In fact the HUD AC group indicated that 875,000 families have been eliminated from the housing market. Not only has the government failed to add new opportunities, it has taken opportunities away from close to 900,000 Canadian families. How can the government be treated seriously? How can Canadians accept the government at its face value? How can Canadians accept the government's word when it engages in contradictory policies which have no sense or substance?
One cannot justify the lack of action, protection and cushioning in a period of intense interest rates when one knows that the Minister of Finance is sitting on his bundle of money which he is prepared to spend foolishly.
I sat here in absolute amazement when the Prime Minister said, "I have got secret information". This is the man who believes in openness. He has secret information indicating that because of the awful job the Liberals have done, he can project the deficit going up to $14 billion.
It is no secret why the deficit is going up to $14 billion. It is the Conservative government which decided to spend $2.3 billion on its mortgage deductibility plan. It is the Conservative government which talked about spending $2.7 billion on the national deficit to buy back Petro-Canada. We know what is causing the deficit; it is their initiatives. It is time the government stopped trying to pawn it off on the previous government. We are asking the government to become concerned about the present and not the past, rather than engaging in frivolous leaps into the fuzzy future about which the Prime Minister likes to talk. He said that we will have oil by 1990, but the people are concerned about what they will pay for oil in 1980. They are concerned about the fact that if the $4 increase goes into effect, they will be paying an additional $300 a month for fuel oil. That is what they are concerned about.
When we asked the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Hnatyshyn), the living example of altruism and obtuseness, what exactly he will do, he said, "I think I have something in the way of a taxation policy". That comes as big news. The minister is providing no assurances. He is providing no security for the people who must face the prospect of substantial heating bill and gas consumption increases because of that $4 increase. In my own province the $4

November 6, 1979
Severe Economic Hardship
increase will pull close to $200 million out of the provincial economy. That is $200 million which we can ill afford.
What answer do we receive from the first minister and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources? They say, "Don't worry, we will make a deal with Mr. Lougheed". 1 know what kind of deal will be made. Mr. Lougheed has said what the deal will be. The only deal Mr. Lougheed will accept is: when he gets all the money he will lend it back to Manitobans at a 12 per cent interest rate. That is the deal Mr. Lougheed wants. It is an interesting example of Tory economics. They take the windfall rents off those resources, transfer them to one province, and lend the money back to other provinces at exorbitant interest rates. How can that so-called energy package be justified? It is a package which has become unstrung and untied very quickly.
The question of pricing is really the key issue at the heart of our non-confidence motion. There is no credibility or acceptance on the part of Canadians concerning the government's energy package, because they know the facts. They know the facts when it comes to those interesting allocations that we will give oil companies.
During question period today, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Prime Minister said that we must rely upon the multinationals to supply us with energy. I have an interesting column which indicates that multinationals are spending their profits, not on exploring for new energy, but for tomato greenhouses in southern Ontario. I have nothing against tomato greenhouses in southern Ontario, but why are they spending the excess profits from natural resources to build subdivisions in Alberta, tomato farms in Ontario, and fast food restaurants along the 401 ?
How can the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources gain any kind of acceptance on the part of the Canadian public when they know that the excess profits now being earned are not being turned back into exploration and development but are being diversified for takeovers, acquisitions, mergers, and new commercial ventures which have nothing to do with energy problems? They call that an energy package; they call that an energy policy? Of course the minister is now prepared to accept that because he has his deals in, he has his arrangements made, yet we know that kind of transfer of wealth, with all the tomato farms in southern Ontario, is only going to the treasuries in New York, Chicago, Geneva and wherever else.
When we are talking about the deficit problem in this country, what is a greater addition to the deficit than additional excess profits to multinational oil corporations which are immediately transferred out of Canada? How do we justify those kinds of profits when this minister gives us no assurance that he is prepared to step in to ensure that the profits will not be used for these extraneous, superfluous purposes, but will in fact be used to gain self-sufficiency? There is no assurance of that kind forthcoming, and again the actions speak much louder than the words.
We note the same kind of arrangement when we consider the pricing arrangement as far as energy is concerned, particularly in terms of development itself and public accountability. I listened again with frank amazement to the first minister today who said we can be sure that the government will set up an institution to take public moneys and reinvest it in energy development. That sounded to me like a pretty good description of Petro-Canada. Why are we going through the silly exercise of ripping Petro-Canada apart, selling off bits and pieces and adding to the public deficit $2.3 billion, in order to set up another institution which is going to do the same thing? Surely members opposite, even those from Alberta, must be able to figure out that this can cause serious duplication and wasted effort.
Let us take the first minister at his own words. Let us have a reversal of his Petro-Canada stand and let us have a windfall profit tax. Let us take the money from that tax and put it into PetroCan so it can invest in new oil developments, tar sands, offshore developments, and renewable resources. That is a great, sensational idea. But, let us do it with the instrument we have and let us not waste time, the taxpayers' money, the efforts of this government and the time of this House wrecking apart a vehicle and a mechanism which is already in place.
Again, how can the government ask people to take it seriously? That is why the two-by-four has to come over the head so we can bring them back to their senses and make them realize what they are really doing. If the first minister is honest and forthright in what he is saying, and I accept that he is, then we say go ahead and do this and we will support him. If the government puts the money into PetroCan, the money it gets from the windfall profit tax, there will be no argument from this side of the House.
We also think there has to be substantial concern about the recycling of those additional, excess profits. There should be a very clear statement about this rather than the fuzzy vagueness we have heard so far about the need for consumer credit. We should recycle this right across the country to ensure that the consumers do not have to bear the full brunt of those increased prices.
It is only a national government with a full range of instruments at its disposal that can undertake that kind of activity. Perhaps the fact that frightens us the most on this side of the House is the same fact that was noted in the report of the Economic Council of Canada, that increasingly the ability of the federal government to manage the economy and to make decisions work in the interest of a number of regions in Canada is being evaporated and eroded by the giveaways and the erosions of the federal structure. That particular process has proceeded faster and further in the last six months than in the last 16 years in this country.
This Prime Minister and this government have given away more power, more jurisdiction, more authority and more instruments, and are talking about doing so even more, than any other government in the history of this country. Yet they turn around and say they want to manage, they want to be tough and they want to be strong. One needs something in his

November 6, 1979

hands in order to do that. One needs some tools to do the job. We cannot get by on empty rhetoric and words. If the first minister of this country thinks he can get by with his acts of friendly persuasion, without having any leverage, anything to call to account and anything to take to the bargaining table, then he is in for a sorry surprise.
I was in the provincial legislature for six years.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext: It shows.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext: Of course it shows. 1 think it is worth while that members opposite hear of some of my experiences. The fact of the matter is that provincial jurisdictions are not large enough and do not have the capacity to make decisions that serve the entire country. I have no bone to pick with Alberta as a province. I think the premier of that province is doing what his mandate tells him to do, which is to defend the interests of Alberta. However, when we are here to defend the interests of all Canadians we must recognize that we cannot allow one province to make economic decisions for the other nine. That is just not right, and the fact of the matter is that one province containing only 8 per cent of the population, and a small part of the land mass, does not have the scope or the ability, or in fact the mandate, to speak for the entire country. Yet we constantly throw back to that province the right to make those decisions.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext: How many Liberals are there there?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext: I would suggest to the hon. member opposite that he should look to the next election because I think there will be a very interesting change taking place in that area.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext:
The member laughs now. I find that interesting, but he should talk to some of his colleagues in that area because they are finding that they are part of a national government which at least presumes to have to take decisions in the national interest, and that is going to start working against those regional parochialisms. People are going to recognize that that sort of favoured Tory straw man that was kicked around western Canada for the last 20 years, called the federal government, is now going to be their government and not ours, and that is going to make a very interesting political change in that province. I suggest to the hon. member that he should really start looking to his own constituency rather than laughing.
The point of the matter is that they cannot govern this country if they are giving it away. They simply cannot govern this country if they are giving its instruments away. Whether they call it the theology of privatization, or the orthodoxy of neo-conservatism, what is really running at cross currents is the philosophical position of a right wing Conservative party with the essential responsibility of governing. I would try to provide hon. members with this suggestion. It is about time they stopped fighting their philosophical battles and started worrying more about where this country is going to go.
Severe Economic Hardship
The Prime Minister talks about the future of Canada, but there will not be much future if there is not a national government to protect and enhance it. There will not be much future if all we have left is the right of the Prime Minister to be invited to meetings of a confederation of provincial barons when they decide to make decisions, and he comes and opens the door. There will not be much future left in this country after we have dismantled and taken apart the taxation and resources of a national reservoir and simply passed this on to the provinces. The government simply cannot make decisions when it does not have the wherewithal and the means to do so.
