subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I appear to be slightly out of breath it is because I was trying to conserve energy and I ran over here. I want to express my appreciation to the opposition for giving me a chance to get involved in this particular debate. On the basis of what transpired this afternoon, 1 thought that we might have points of order and points of privilege extending right up until the time of the vote. I was concerned that these points of discussion might intrude on my time. 1 know that there are hon. members who want to make a full contribution to the issues involved in this particular motion. I know that my colleagues on this side of the House are interested in participating, so I will try not to take any more time than is necessary.

November 6, 1979
Severe Economic Hardship
Today in the course of the question period and in enquiries made by my colleagues in the Social Credit party, there were some questions raised with regard to the supply situation in eastern Canada. These are questions to which I have addressed myself during the five months I have occupied this portfolio. I would like to spend some time this evening reporting to this House with respect to the actual situation. 1 am concerned about the approach taken by the official opposition with regard to this particular topic, because it seems to be trying to sow fear and apprehension in the minds of Canadians.
1 want Canadians to know that I too am concerned about our supply situation. This is not a new concern for me because I was concerned during the time I was in opposition. Upon taking over this portfolio, I took steps with respect to this very serious problem. It does little good for the members who made up the previous government, and who bear a responsibility for the circumstances in which we find ourselves today, to raise phantom concerns in the minds of the Canadian people. I want to bring to the attention of this House some of the facts that I have gone into in my assessment of the current situation and the outlines of some of the objectives, as I see them, for our national energy policy, some of which were articulated so well by the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) this afternoon.
Despite strenuous efforts to limit Canada's need for oil imports in recent months, it is projected that in the fourth quarter in 1979, one quarter of our national oil requirements will be imported. These projections suggest that the provinces from Ontario eastward will rely on foreign oil for over one third of their requirements. Canadian demand for oil products has continued to grow. In the January to September, 1979, period demand for oil products was 3.4 per cent higher than in the same period in 1978. Gasoline use was 4.3 per cent higher.
The petroleum products supply outlook reflects the rapid rate of consumption in the January to September period. Refineries in Canada produced 6 per cent more gasoline in that period than in the same period in 1978. Even so, gasoline stocks this September remained lower than in September, 1978. Production of heating oil in preparation for the coming winter is almost 11 per cent above January to September, 1978, production. Yet stocks this September remain below the September, 1978, level. The level of heating oil inventory is important to assure adequate supplies for unusually long cold periods. However, the current situation is not a crisis. It is tight but manageable.
Canada should have access to sufficient supplies from imported and domestic crude oil and petroleum products to satisfy demands as currently projected. On the basis of the steps which have been taken by myself and the government, and the steps we intend to take with respect to our objective of energy self-sufficiency and restraining demand and, in fact, with respect to increasing supply in Canada, we hope to lead Canada to a new possibility and a new potential for the 1980s.
Unlike the previous government and its seat of the pants approach to energy management, this government has taken concrete and specific actions to ensure that Canadians do indeed get through this winter with adequate supplies of

heating oil. Some of these actions were referred to in the House today. They include increased production of domestic crude, and a reduction in exports of oil exports of crude to the United States. The reduction will go down in November from 55,000 barrels a day to virtually nil or nominal exports. The purpose of this is to provide Canadian refineries with a maximum quantity of Canadian crude supplies.
They include a change in the allocation system of the Interprovincial Pipe Line to allow independents access to this Canadian crude supply. In November of this year independents will have access to upwards of 5,000 barrels of oil a day each to supply the people of Quebec and eastern Canada under the new approach which is being taken with respect to Interprovincial Pipe Line allocations from western Canada. I have referred on a number of occasions to a telex which I sent out on August 15 this year. In that message I made quite clear to refiners and terminal operators in this country that I expected fair and equitable treatment for the independents of our country, to ensure that there would be no attempt to grab a larger share of the market. I continue to monitor the situation.
A very important element in refining with respect to the initiative we are taking is that my department consults, and will continue to do so fully and frequently, with the provincial governments, the refiners, and the independents so as to maximize the flexibility of our supplies and transportation systems. It should not be necessary for me to take these actions. Unfortunately, however, they were required because of the ineptitude of the previous government and its inability to provide energy leadership and energy management.
I want to deal also with the question of the emergency allocation legislation, Mr. Speaker. I have indicated that there is no crisis and no emergency in our country today. We know the terms of that legislation, Mr. Speaker. It requires that if there is such a situation, then there must be a declaration which will be referred to Parliament for consideration.
Should we be faced with a disruption in supply or an emergency situation in Canada, I can assure this House that the government is prepared to use the powers available to it, in order to conserve supplies and provide for their equitable distribution. In this regard I have indicated, in answer to questions in the House, that I intend as a matter of course and without any indication that there is a particular emergency in Canada at the time of introducing administrative amendments to the Energy Supplies Emergency Act 1979, to announce appointments to the Energy Supplies Allocation Board. Part of the responsibilities of this board will be to co-ordinate activities with respect to supply matters and to plan for a possible emergency. It is not intended, by making appointments to this board, to indicate that there is an emergency. I am taking this action only out of an abundance of caution, and will likely make the appointments at the time of the introduction of the amendments.
It should be underlined again that a support structure has been put in place, in case of an emergency. My department has
November 6, 1979

been consulting fully with the provinces and with the industry, as well as with those people who are involved in transportation.
A support basis is available to them so that they can move quickly and firmly in the event of an emergency.
I think we should examine the realities of Canadian oil prices and assess our position in the context of a national energy policy. Canadian oil prices are more than $10 per barrel below the cost of imports, and about $8.50 per barrel below the average cost of crude in Chicago. Canadian oil is now further below the international price than at any time since 1973.
These low prices for crude, combined with an exceptionally light level of taxation of petroleum products compared to other western countries, provide Canadian consumers with the lowest petroleum product prices of any major industrialized country. For example, at the end of September, 1979, the average price of gasoline sold in Canada was approximately $1.05 per gallon, significantly below the $1.37 which the average U.S. consumer paid for a comparable gallon of gasoline. Compared to other European countries, the low comparative price Canadians pay for gasoline is even more evident. For example, in the United Kingdom the average price of gasoline at the end of September of this year was $2.59 per gallon, in West Germany $3.17 per gallon, in France $3.62 per gallon, and in Italy $3.75 per gallon. Canadian prices do not compare with prices in other countries and, in fact, are much lower. Canadians now pay less for gasoline in real terms that they did in the 1950s.
Canadians intuitively realize the bargain that oil products are in this country and, as a result, have not reduced their demand because there has been no incentive to do so. The signals that the marketplace and the former government were providing to the Canadian consumer, were the wrong signals. Instead of saying, "Slow down, it is expensive and needs to be saved", the past government's policy implicitly said, "Go ahead, use more, it is really a bargain."
The pricing policy of the previous government was a $1 per barrel increase every six months in the wellhead price of crude. A continuation of this policy would see Canadian prices continue to fall further behind international levels. While it is difficult to forecast international prices accurately, it is expected that the present policy would lead to a price gap between domestic and international prices of about $13.00 per barrel in 1985.

speechtext: What is wrong with that?

speechtext:
I would ask the hon. member to go back to Regina and ask the premier of his province what is wrong with it. He would be told very clearly what is wrong.
On imported oil, this gap would have to be covered by federal government subsidies under the oil import compensation program. On the basis of the former government's policies, by 1985 the federal government would have to pay almost $4 billion in oil import compensation because of the difference between the international and the domestic prices. The needless payment of Canadian funds of this magnitude into foreign
Severe Economic Hardship
hands is something that the Canadian government cannot condone, and the Canadian economy certainly cannot bear this burden. Canadians in this situation would, in effect, be paying $4 billion in one year for foreign oil and, most important, would be forgoing the opportunity of developing domestic resources and moving Canada towards oil self-sufficiency.
The goal of this government, as has been stated many times in the House and outside it, is to achieve energy self-sufficiency by 1990. For a country with the energy potential such as Canada has, any lesser goal would not be acceptable to the Canadian people. It is the intention of this government to get us to energy self-sufficiency and, in the course of that, to increase Canadian ownership and participation in resource development.
During the last two months I have had intensive negotiations and consultations with the provinces regarding the development of a comprehensive energy package and its crucial pricing component. There are important elements with respect to our energy package that I want to bring to the attention of the House tonight.
First, the domestic price of Canadian crude oil must increase faster than it has in the past. Second, petroleum products sold in Canada must be priced more realistically than they are today. Third, Canada's abundant supplies of natural gas must be substituted for oil as much as possible. Fourth, the petroleum industry in Canada must be encouraged to develop Canadian petroleum resources as quickly as possible. Fifth, more Canadians must be encouraged to participate in the resource development of their country. Sixth, the federal government and the provinces must actively encourage an acceleration of energy projects in Canada. Seventh, new initiatives to promote and encourage conservation by Canadians must be developed. Eighth, offset measures must be introduced to counteract as much as possible the economic effects that higher prices will cause to those least able to absorb them.
That is the basis of the energy policy that this government is bringing forward; that is the basis of the policy to which we are committed in this House.
I think it would be appropriate to review, in the context of the motion placed before us today, a statement with respect to the policies of the former government, the party moving this particular resolution. Its terms are vague and they are rather equivocal. I suggest we should examine the position of the former government with respect to energy policy and oil pricing in Canada over the years.
Last week the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Trudeau) told hon. members that the current pricing agreement with Alberta was sufficient and that no new agreement was necessary. I think that was the essence of the representation he made and the position he put forward in the course of his remarks. I have already outlined some of the consequences of that policy: increased oil demand, more reliance on foreign oil, higher oil compensation payments, and no chance for oil self-sufficiency. The former government referred to this policy as "energy self-reliance". Whatever it is, it is certainly not oil self-suffic-

iency. Times have really changed as far as the former government is concerned.
Let us examine the Liberal record, Mr. Speaker. On December 6, 1973, in a debate in this Elouse on petroleum policy, the then prime minister, now Leader of the Opposition, outlined his government's national oil policy objective as follows:
The object is Canadian self-sufficiency in oil and oil products before the end of this decade.
Times have really changed, Mr. Speaker, as far as the position of the Liberals is concerned. In March, 1974, the then minister of energy, mines and resources, making a statement on oil and gas policy, said:
The most fundamental principle which the federal government would like to advance is to sustain the capacity for continuing self-sufficiency.
We would propose that western well-head prices rise ... to equivalent international prices now prevailing in Montreal.
And again in April, 1975, at the federal-provincial first ministers' conference, the Leader of the Opposition said:
We cannot expect those who search for oil-whether they be Canadian or other-to look for it and develop it in Canada if our prices arc far below those in other countries .. . We cannot expect Alberta and Saskatchewan to go on year after year selling their oil to Canadians at a price which is far below what they could get by exporting it. So my colleagues in the government and I have come reluctantly to believe that the price of oil in Canada must go up-toward the world price.

Mr. Speaker, I conclude my remarks by simply pointing out that in terms of Canada's energy policy we have a great potential in this country. Frankly, I take a rather different attitude from that taken by the opposition in the context of its motion. They have taken a negative, defeatist approach with respect to oil policy and have not presented any clear alternative, or any alternative at all. Instead, their attitude is one that merely criticizes situations that have not yet occurred and are not taking place at the present time.
In Canada we can achieve energy self-sufficiency. It is a possibility for us. It is not an arduous or an onerous obligation. It is a possibility that will result in a decade of progress, and a decade in which we in Canada can and should develop our energy resources. We should take advantage of this in a non-partisan way as much as possible. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say at the outset that my speech will be very brief. I share the feelings just expressed by the minister, that we are here in a non-partisan way and that we have proposals to make to the government to help it improve the energy policy. I am very happy to have this opportunity to participate in the debate because it deals with a matter which is of the utmost importance to Canada.
The whole question of energy, its availability and its price all affect the life of every individual and every company in every sector of our society and economy. Therefore, the importance of this debate cannot be overestimated.
The other aspect of this debate that strikes me tonight is the profound difference that lies between my party, the Liberal party, and the Conservative government on the issue of energy as well as on other subjects. Mr. Speaker, how often have we heard remarks and comments by our friends on my left, on the far left, to the effect that both the Progressive Conservative Party and the Liberal party carry the same message. They like to say we are one and the same. But I reject this and indeed the difference between our two parties appears clearly in this debate tonight. It appears in the approach we have towards society, toward responsibility of the government.
As I said, the difference between our two parties is obvious and so is the concept we have of society and of our role. At the same time, one must admit that to a certain extent we do share the same philosophy. I can give you an example. The Progressive Conservative Party merely carries on with the economic policy without presenting a new budget, it is quite satisfied with ours.
Besides, just like the Progessive Conservatives we believe that the private sector is the main driving force within our society. We must give impetus to the economy of our private sector and stimulate the open market, but we are not so radical about it as some of our hon. friends opposite. And when we see that some people are unfairly treated, that there are no equal opportunities for everyone across the country, that some people cannot defend themselves, then we do not hesitate to intervene to protect them and ensure the safety of each and every Canadian. That is the fundamental difference between the two parties. And I hope our hon. friends to our left will realize this difference because, as I said earlier in my remarks, it is quite evident in the case of the energy crisis in Canada.
The Progressive Conservative Party has always been the party which fought to defend special interests in Canada, having neither the capability nor perhaps the will to offer us- and when I say us, I mean the Canadian people-programs likely to benefit all Canadians. As an example of this, Mr. Speaker, I shall mention the nearly complete absence of a social program on the platform of the Progressive Conservative Party when it held power before and even after the war, as well as when it was in the opposition. I cannot say the same
November 6, 1979

thing about our hon. friends to our left, but from the Progressive Conservative Party, nothing.
Now, the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) would like to create the impression that his party has abandoned its traditional position in order to move more to the centre, but during this debate on energy tonight in the House. Mr. Speaker, we have come to realize that nothing has changed and that his party still represents special interests just as before.

What are these special interests that this government represents in this debate? Of course three immediately come to mind. First, obviously, are those who are interested in an accelerated rise to world prices, as opposed to the Liberal policy of organized slow rise toward prices on the international level. Obviously the oil companies are interested in that, the companies and persons associated with oil companies. Who can blame them?
Second, there is of course a certain provincial government that is particularly interested in a rapid increase in oil prices to world levels. Then there is the federal government itself. They are interested in finding ways to finance, for example, the mortgage tax credit scheme to which my friend from Winnipeg made reference earlier in his remarks.
Beyond that, what about Canadians at large? What about the small businessman? What about individuals? What about the poor? Those in the poor areas of my riding are concerned-

He laughs because he knows nothing about my riding, Saint-Henri-Westmount, but I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that we have much poverty in some areas.

What of those people? Is this policy of a rapid rise to world levels really in their interest? Is it really in the interest of all Canadians, or is it a classic Tory position of being interested in special interest groups? In this case there are the three that I cited, the companies and the governments of Canada at the provincial and federal levels.
What of other Canadians? Do they not have reason to be outraged at the fact that here is a Canadian natural resource they can buy as easily from an international cartel as they can at the same price from their own country? Are they not going to question the advantages of being Canadian? What are these resources for that we have in Canada, if they are not to stimulate and provide some kind of competitive advantage for Canadians?
What do they tell us? They say, "It is good for you," that it is "a long-term remedy," that "you may freeze, you may go bankrupt and you may not be able to travel, but the optimistic side is that in the long term it is good for you." I suppose this is not unlike the message that was delivered to the Christian heretics as they stood at the stake, the optimistic message was
Severe Economic Hardship
that in the long term it was good for them. That is the kind of situation we are facing in this energy issue.
Let me carry this one step further. Referring back to the comments of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Trudeau) this afternoon, he made reference to the cartel, and a cartel it is, the OPEC cartel. I am not criticizing the legality of that cartel. Under our Combines Investigation Act, as I recall it, we do accept a cartel at the international level for our exports. However, domestically our law dealing with cartels, or what is known as price fixing, is perhaps the most serious crime in the Combines Investigation Act.
This government is telling us that we are to follow this cartel which would be illegal under our domestic law. If any companies in Canada engaged in such an outrageous cartel, the officers responsible would be put in jail. However, we are told that we are to follow the artificial prices set by this cartel.
Frankly, I find this shocking, even coming from a Conservative government. If we go back to the nineteenth century, to the unfettered free enterprise system, monopolies and cartels were the order of the day. It may be that our Conservative friends are seeking their historical roots.
We are dealing with a cartel. As far as I am concerned, we have no business tying Canadian domestic prices to cartel prices in any way, shape or form.
We heard about conservation from the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Hnatyshyn). He said the Liberal government had encouraged Canadians to "go ahead," and I wrote down the words, "and use more, it's really a bargain." Those are the words he used. That is not my impression of what the Liberal government was telling the people of Canada. In fact conservation measures had been foremost in the minds of the Liberal government and in the message they conveyed to the Canadian people.
I suggest there is no evidence, but perhaps the government has some to offer, that increased prices will create conservation. When I was a student in Lrance in the late fifties, gas cost $1 a gallon. I do not know how many here have driven around Place de la Concorde or anywhere else in Paris or Europe. There is no evidence that people have conserved. There is evidence that they have sorted out their priorities and they probably compromise in some other area of their lives rather than sacrifice their automobiles which, of course, are fundamental to the infrastructure of society in this country. Therefore, to talk conservation in these terms is absolute rubbish.
We are told that the rising price of oil will make us look for more resources. We are told that if we follow the shock treatment and increase prices, people will be conscious of the fact we have to find other sources of energy, that that is the message we have to get across.

Let us be serious, Mr. Speaker. I am convinced that Canadians today are well aware of the fact that there is an energy crisis. They do not need an electric stimulus like mice to react. I find that it is an entirely stupid argument. The Canadian

November 6, 1979
Severe Economic Hardship
people are very aware of their own priorities and the national priorities. I would like, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian government also to be aware of them.

What about exploration, new frontier exploration in particular? That is something I have not heard discussed in this debate. Of course I was absent from the House for part of the day. What are we doing about new frontier exploration? Rising prices are supposed to stimulate that. We have some very major fiscal policies in place to stimulate development in the new frontier. Canadian development expenses can be written off at 30 per cent on the declining balance. Canadian exploration expenses are deductible at 100 per cent.
We have in addition to that, depletion. We have depletion of $1 for every $3 earned, which is the normal depreciation. Beyond that we have super depletion which gives the additional $2. In fact there are circumstances where there is no money at risk in drilling for oil on the new frontier at the present time under our fiscal system. Now we are being asked to compound that by bringing the price to world levels. Surely there has to be a trade-off here somewhere. Canadian taxpayers are already paying an exceedingly heavy price for oil development in the new frontier. That seems to have been forgotten by those in the benches across the aisle. Perhaps it is the right program. Perhaps those fiscal programs have stimulated an enormous amount of drilling in those areas where obviously the risk is high.
However, there has to be a rationalization. If these gentlemen are prepared to let Canadian oil prices domestically rise to world prices, surely we have to reassess the fiscal implications of that on the other side of the balance sheet. To my knowledge that has not been done.
What bothers me about this whole debate is that I really did not hear gentlemen on the other side speaking for Canadians. Our leader has often said they do not believe someone should speak for Canadians, but surely in this House we have a responsibility to speak for Canadians.
Canadians do not understand why they should have to pay world prices for resources which are theirs, resources which companies are permitted to extract with enormous tax benefits. I do not regard it as any kind of rip-off to permit Canadians to have some kind of competitive advantages. They have enough disadvantages. They have distance. They have climate. They are caught up with all the other problems of this country, and here we have one advantage we can confer on them as we have done in certain cases with respect to hydro electricity. But no, we have to go to world prices in the name of conservation, in the name of looking for alternative sources of energy, all of which I agree with, particularly looking for alternate sources of energy, because, as we know, conservation is a short-term proposition at best. We have to find other sources of energy, and the situation I drew to your attention earlier, Mr. Speaker, means Canadians are conscious of that; they are prepared to make that investment, they know that problem, and they are going to move in that direction.

Let us for once, in this debate, talk about people. Speakers from this side of the House have, and I carry that over to my friends in the New Democratic Party. I do not think I am essentially considered a left-wing sympathizer, but I am realistic about what the opportunities are in this country and I think I am realistic about what we should be doing in terms of protecting Canadians against the disastrous effect of inflation in terms of our competitiveness, in terms of putting upward pressure on rate settlements and so on, if we follow the policy which this government is apparently following, namely, to force oil prices up to world levels as quickly as possible.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have before us today a motion standing in the name of the Liberal party which says that this House has no confidence in the government because of their bungling of various aspects of the national energy policy, namely, the possibility of a home heating oil shortage this winter, a high energy price policy, and a high interest rate policy.
I should like to ask members of the Liberal party, who was in power for the last 11 years while this situation with regard to energy and high interest rate policy was allowed to deteriorate? It did not happen over night and these problems did not just begin with the Conservative government. They only continued with the Conservative party once it obtained office. Who was it who allowed the multinational oil companies over the past decade to control 90 per cent of the oil industry in this country, hence preventing the present government from getting a handle on national energy policy and the direction we should be taking in the development of our oil industry and prices fixed for its products?
Indeed, even with the establishment of Petro-Canada, 80 per cent of the oil industry still remains in foreign hands. That is an indictment of the energy policy or so-called energy policy of the Liberal party while it was in power. Indeed, it was that party in the late sixties which allowed these same oil companies to export half our total production of oil to the United States, thus contributing to the very shortages we are facing today. It is also the Liberal government, as stated in its energy policy in 1976, which said their policy was to move toward world prices. So the only difference between the Liberals and the Conservatives is that the Conservatives are going to do it in one big jump while the Liberals were going to do it gradually. So it is very hypocritical of them to argue, now they are in opposition, that we should not move toward the world price demanded by the OPEC cartel. That is the very policy the Liberal minister of energy was defending while his party was in power.
If we turn to the other aspect of the motion before us tonight, criticizing the government for its failure to deal with the potential shortage of home heating oil, who was it who allowed the National Energy Board last year to increase exports of oil products to the United States thereby contributing to shortages we may face this winter in home heating oil? It was the Liberal government.
If we think back to interest rate policy, it was the Liberal government which began the increases in interest rates seven
November 6, 1979

times in 1979 before the last May election, and the Conservatives are only continuing the interest rate policy begun by the Liberals. Yet here in this motion we find the Liberal opposition criticizing the Conservative government for following the same policy. I can only conclude that the motion we have before us is a desperate act by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Trudeau) in an attempt to give the impression somehow that this defeated party is the real opposition in the House. I believe the people of Canada in the past month have seen through that kind of hypocrisy and that kind of duplicity.

We have the spectacle of the Leader of the Opposition, this Ozymandias of the Liberal party, a party now discovering that his feet are of clay, desperately trying to rally his troops behind him to think that he is the real opposition though we know that he is leading a party that is disillusioned, bankrupt of any principle, and bankrupt of any policy for this country. This was evident in the last general election.
If the Leader of the Opposition has discovered he has feet of clay I think it has become evident that the people of Canada have discovered that the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) has a head of clay when it comes to national energy policy.
I am reminded of the story of the three party leaders flying over one of those unstable South American countries. The plane crashed, but fortunately all three survived. In their attempt to escape from the jungle they were captured by a group of revolutionaries who saw them as interlopers and wanted to put them to death before a firing squad. Well, they took them out one at a time, and the first was the leader of the NDP. They lined him up against the wall and just as they were about to give the order to the firing squad to shoot, the NDP leader came up with an idea for a plan to escape and shouted "Earthquake! Earthquake!" The firing squad dropped their rifles and scattered for cover and the leader was able to escape.
Meanwhile, Mr. Trudeau and Mr. Clark were watching through the prison windows and decided they had better try something, too, because, of course, they were next before the firing squad. The Leader of the Opposition was taken out and he quickly decided he must think of a plan of escape and, just as they were about to fire, he shouted "Volcano! Volcano!". Again the firing squad dropped their rifles and ran, and he was able to escape.
Meanwhile, the Prime Minister was sweating behind the bars because he knew he was next. He was called out, the firing squad was lined up ready to shoot, and he came up with a brilliant plan of escape. He shouted "Fire! fire!".

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish we could light a fire beneath this government in terms of an energy policy. We were promised last August that a national energy policy would be coming forward. We have not seen it to date. Instead, we have seen drift and incompetence, and indeed a kind of pricing policy which, I predict, will become public on Monday when the first ministers' conference is drawn and we as Canadians, as I said in the House the other day, will get a horrendous Christmas present from the Prime Minister in terms of energy pricing.
This government is determined to move to world prices as soon as possible, and in reports that I have received, I find their plans are to move to the world price, or close to it, by 1983. The price facing Canadians in that year will be $29.75 a barrel for oil, an increase of some 120 per cent over the current price of $13.75 a barrel. That kind of dramatic escalation in oil prices in Canada will not achieve the goal that this government has argued it will, namely, self-sufficiency, but instead will cause the most severe recession and economic dislocation that this country has seen in modern times. That is why we argue that it is folly to pay a price escalation on an artificial cartel price, namely, OPEC's. Instead, we will argue, and have been arguing, that we should base it on the real cost of bringing on new supplies in Canada, and phase in a price increase in a way that the economy and the consumer can absorb it.
If we proceed with this government's plan to escalate to the world price, or to 90 per cent of it as soon as possible, that means that by 1983 Canadian consumers will be paying an extra $700 a year just to heat their homes and drive their cars. I think that this is a burden for people faced with already high inflation; it is unjustifiable, illogical, and should not be proceeded with by this government.
We also know that this government is bent on destroying one of the most successful options we have in the oil industry, namely, Petro-Canada. The government wants to dismantle it, to privatize it, to let go an effective tool that the federal government has in national energy planning and development. The government is arguing that the private sector can do it better than a Crown corporation, and the private sector, and others have argued as well as I have, for reasons to keep Petro-Canada.
Let me quote a good summary of why we should keep Petro-Canada. It reads:
Petro-Canada supplements the job being done by the private sector and takes appropriate risks where the private sector is reluctant. Petro-Canada provides Canadians with a better insight into the complexity of finding and developing new oil and gas reserves.
Petro-Canada can and should, along with the private petroleum industry, play a leadership role in achieving crude oil self-sufficiency for Canada by 1995.
... urges the federal government not to "reprivatize" Petro-Canada but to retain essential functions within a national petroleum company.

This reliance on the private sector which I have described really means reliance on the multinational oil companies which have a stranglehold on the oil industry in Canada. Both the Liberals and the Conservatives accept the kind of tax policies that have been put in place over the past decade, tax policies which benefit these companies, and both have accepted the high profits over the years that these companies have been making at the expense of Canadian consumers. Only recently, in the past few days, do I get some inkling from the Liberal party that there may be something wrong with these extraordinarily high profits. I wish I had heard that a couple of years ago when the profits were increasing at almost the same rate.
Indeed, it was the Liberal government that implemented a tax regime that is still being followed by the present Conservative government, which means that for every $1 the oil companies spend on exploration in Canada, we, the taxpayers, put up 65 cents in terms of tax concessions given to these multinational oil companies operating in Canada. What do we get in return? We certainly do not get any kind of ownership or control in the way they exploit this resource which belongs to the people of Canada. Contrast that with the role of Petro-Canada which we, as Canadians, own, and the ability we have, through Petro-Canada, to take some real action in the interests of Canadians without the kind of blackmail tactics which the multinationals have adopted in the past.
Indeed, we have seen the Liberal government, again supported by the Conservatives when they were in opposition, allowing these oil companies to accumulate up to the end of 1978 a total of $1.5 billion in deferred taxes, taxes which have not been paid to the federal treasury. If the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) wants to look for a source of funds to reduce the deficit, I will tell him it is right there before his very eyes.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

It is the former Liberal government which allowed-a policy continued by the present Conservative government-the effective tax rate of the multinational companies, with their record profits, to decline from 35 per cent in 1974 to 21 per cent in 1978. Indeed, Shell Canada, which in 1978 made a profit of $151 million, paid not one cent of federal income tax. That was the kind of tax policies that these

two old line parties adopted in the past, and I find it utterly hypocritical for the Liberal party in its motion today to criticize the Conservatives for doing the very same thing they did.

Indeed we have in the private sector, which this Prime Minister wants to develop, Imperial, Shell, Texaco and Gulf which were allowed to increase their profits by $880 million, an increase of 55 per cent. We will get only more of the same from the two old line parties in terms of their attitude toward the private sector.
The motion before us criticizes the government on the issue of home heating supplies for the winter. On October 15 I raised this very issue with the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Hnatyshyn), and I pointed out to him that in my province of Ontario home heating oil reserves are down 20 per cent over the same period last year, and we have, in the most recent report from the National Energy Board, a situation where all oil products have declined some 8.3 per cent as of October 1. What are the reasons for this decline?
We hear of refinery breakdowns, we hear that the pipelines are at maximum capacity, and that there is a scarcity of foreign supply at short notice. We do not hear very much about an investigation that has been taking place for the past six years, carried out by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, of collusion and price fixing in the oil industry in Canada. I should like to see that study come to light so that we may judge for ourselves whether or not there is, by way of collusion, a manipulation of supply that is contributing to a potential shortage over the winter, and yet we have no report forthcoming from this government.
We also find that the reason to which I alluded earlier for this potential shortage is that the National Energy Board has allowed exports of oil products to increase some 21 per cent between January and mid-summer of this year, and again that kind of increase took place under the regime of the former Liberal government which is now criticizing the new government for failing to have enough oil on hand.
When the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources says the situation is fragile, it is an indication that he has no contingency plans in place, or at least has not made them public to the House and the people of Canada. We can only conclude that he is giving us a bland assurance, rather than some concrete evidence that the mechanisms are now in place to move fuel oil quickly from one region of the country to another in order to face eventual shortages.
I fear for the consumers of eastern Canada, especially those in Quebec and the maritimes, this winter in the event of a possible disruption of supply. I learned tonight that the Iranian government has stopped loading American tankers with oil. I hope we do not face another Exxon situation, as we did last spring when the multinational oil companies began to reduce

Canadian allotments from their supply pools in order to meet shortages in other markets.
The government must implement a policy which makes some sense. We agree with the motion, that the government has not met the criteria which we advocated in terms of what an energy policy should be. In light of the state of the economy, there should be a current freeze on energy prices. When we move the price up, any increase beyond the present price should go into a national energy development fund so that we will be assured these moneys will be spent on energy development in Canada to meet Canadian interests.
We would have a commission to investigate oil company prices and profits to ensure that consumers were not ripped off.
We would preserve Petro-Canada, promote alternative energy, and a massive conservation program. We have not seen this forthcoming from the government, and for these reasons we will vote against it tonight.

They were not seized then and they are not seized today of the urgency of the oil situation in the country. I remind hon. members of that. There were many more important matters in this country than getting oil to Quebec and eastern Canada, according to the leader of the then government. Certainly the urgency of the oil situation was not among the reasons cited by the then government.
Of course it is not clear what the direct impact or effect of increased prices will be on demand. Those who have followed our problems will recognize the shallowness and superficiality of that as an argument with respect to the need on the part of this country to move toward world prices.

The manner in which the Liberal party sees the intelligence of the people of this country is something to behold. Not one member opposite gives anyone in the country the benefit of having a bit of brains or intelligence. They do not have the time of day to consider the impact of not moving seriously.
Oil is a finite product. We may be the most fortunate of all western nations. We may have enough energy in the form of oil, coal, gas, hydro, solar power, and bio-mass energy to last us well into the next century, and probably well beyond that, but oil is finite. The former minister of energy, mines and resources, Mr. Gillespie, failed to recognize that in each of his major pronouncements with regard to oil supplies in this country. He failed to recognize that throughout the years that he served in that portfolio, and the consequence of that failure is that this country will face oil shortages in the 1980s. There is no question about that. Whose fault is that? Who has to take the ultimate blame and responsibility? I suggest there is no question but that it is the responsibility of that minister and his government.
What they failed to do in six years we cannot do in five months, but we will do it in eight or ten months. We will turn around the thinking in this country. We will turn it around so as to encourage true conservation through the substitution of other energy forms for oil, through effective home insulation programs and all of the other things that tend to provide protection and balance. We will turn this around so that this country, not by the turn of the century as the Leader of the Opposition and the former minister of energy, mines and resources would have it, is self-sufficient some time after the turn of the century-we will have self-sufficiency in this country by 1990 and we will accomplish that through conservation of our oil, through the development of additional conventional oil, through tertiary improvement and recovery of those oil resources, through the development of frontier oil both in the north and off the coast of eastern Canada, and we will do that by whatever means are necessary. We will not do it on the backs of those people who cannot afford it, as some hon. members over there would have us believe.
The Prime Minister of this country has said on a hundred occasions that he is aware of the situation and that his

government intends to move to protect those people who would be most directly affected by increases in the direction of world oil prices. No one in this chamber knows the situation better than I, and I am glad to note in the gallery the presence of the minister of finance and the minister of development for the province of Nova Scotia. They will tell you, if you want to ask them, that maritimers are already paying twice the national average for domestic electricity. The Prime Minister of this country has said this is not acceptable, that it should be lower. He has indicated that the minimum that is acceptable to this government is domestic electricity rates for the maritimes that do not increase any more than the national average.
Where is the great impact? The cost will not increase. Where was the minister when he was needed? Where was the former minister of regional economic expansion when we needed money for coal? Where were you when Devco wanted resources? Where were you, and what were you doing? What was your leader doing?
What happened in respect of Donkin, Lingan and Devco? What did the former government do about the use of coal to back out oil? Where were you at that time, and what did you do? Where are the new coal mines? Are they in place? Where are the additional plants for the generation of electricity, using coal? You did not do anything about these things because you did not care; you didn't give a damn. Our minister of energy cares and our Prime Minister cares.

What there is in Canada today is a potential shortage of oil and a potential major crisis at any moment. We noted today that Iran has stopped loading oil, some of which presumably is destined for eastern Canada.
Let me talk for a minute or two about the critical situation that faces eastern Canada. For six or seven years, since 1973, the former government ignored the situation. That government was seized of the absolute knowledge that it must store strategic oil five years ago, in 1974. What did that government do? Where is the development at Port Hawkesbury? Where is the development of the mines at Belle Isle, Newfoundland? Where is the storage in Atlantic Canada as a result of pre-planning? It takes three to four years to put in place good, positive, strategic storage capacity. That government knew in 1974 and 1975 that this had to be done. That government had the opportunity to piggyback on U.S. strategic reserve planning, but that government procrastinated.
Who is suffering today? Where is the potential for suffering and for harm? I suggest it is in Atlantic Canada. It exists in the eastern part of the former minister's own province. What good are all his words this afternoon when there is no oil to put in storage in those parts of Atlantic Canada that require storage this fall before freeze-up, in order to have supplies
November 6, 1979

throughout the winter? What happens if the oil is not in place? Whose fault will that be? I suggest it will be the former government s fault because they did not move with storage. They did not move in respect of strategic storage.
Mr. Gillespie, the former minister of energy, told me in response to a question back at the time of the Iranian crisis; "Don't worry about it, son; we will look after it." He did not do much of a job. That minister and his government did not do much of a job. That is all I have to say. They did not put much storage in place. They did not move in respect of coal liquefaction. They did not move with regard to fluidized beds. They did not move with regard to Fundy tidal power. They did not move in respect of a demonstration project on the Annapolis River.
For years there has been $9.5 million in banks in Nova Scotia for the purpose of getting into low head electrical generation. Did that government use the money for that purpose? Where is that money now? It is sitting in the Bank of Nova Scotia in Nova Scotia, instead of being out invested in the production of electricity. Where do we get our electricity? We get it from oil powered generating plants. Where do we get that oil? Every drop of it comes from offshore.
For the first time in ten years there is a government in this country which is concerned about the situation and in fact is doing something about it.

Mr. Speaker, this motion deals with both energy supplies and interest rates. I think that my colleagues who have spoken have dealt most effectively with the Conservative efforts to raise our energy prices in Canada rapidly to world levels, something that will be most harmful to Canadian consumers and Canadian businesses. In fact the hon. member who just spoke forgot to point out that Premier Davis of Ontario has also spoken most effectively against the ideas put forward by the government in this debate. If the government wants to get advice from someone of its own party, I suggest that it stop listening to Premier Lougheed and start listening to Premier Davis.
This evening I want to speak particularly about interest rates, because they are not, in fact, something that is remote from the daily lives of Canadians. Interest rates are costs, and costs are a part of prices. They affect everything done by Canadians and their families. The present record level of interest rates, which is supported by Conservative policy, cuts back the ability of Canadians to buy goods and services of all kinds-cars, homes, food and clothing, everything people need. These high interest rates cut back the ability of factories and businesses generally to expand, to create more production and jobs. These high interest rates limit the ability of business, especially small business, simply to operate at basic non-inflationary levels. Therefore these high interest rates mean losses
1030

November 6, 1979
Severe Economic Hardship
of production and jobs now and over the coming winter months.
The Conservative government has been saying that these high interest rates are needed to fight inflation, but they in themselves drive up costs and add to inflation. The Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) said when he was still leader of the opposition only last March 2, "record high interest rates virtually guarantee more inflation by bidding up the price of money itself'. How soon they forget! All this has been demonstrated by the jump in the cost of living last month of one full point, obviously incorporating increases in costs due to increases in interest rates. The government has allowed these increases to go into effect in the period since it has been in office.
However, even if high interest rates do fight inflation, why should we have the same interest rates which the Americans say are required to fight inflation in their country? Our inflation is some five points lower than inflation in the United States. The government also says that high interest rates are needed to finance the deficit in the balance of payments and to maintain the exchange value of our dollar and that, therefore, we must keep in step with the United States. This deficit is there mainly because we have been sending out more interest and principal to repay previous borrowings for this purpose. It is a never ending treadmill, and the Conservatives want to keep us on it forever.
The deficit is also there because of the high level of foreign control of our economy, which means that we are sending out tremendous amounts of interest, dividends, management fees and the like, to foreign parent companies.
A week or so ago the Americans said they had made a mistake in applying their monetary policy. They thought that their money supply had grown by $3 billion and that therefore they had to raise their interest rates again. Then they found that their money supply had not gone up by $3 billion and that they did not need to raise their interest rates. Surely this American error helps to show the folly of the government continuing to raise our interest rates almost in lock-step with the United States. Upon learning of this error, Henry Reuss, the respected chairman of the banking committee of the U.S. House of Representatives, said that "it was a monumental goof and a monetary Three Mile Island". Surely we cannot let the Conservative government create an economic Three Mile Island for Canadians and their families this winter.
This government should be tackling the basic structural problems of our economy through an industrial strategy to make it more productive and efficient, including dealing with problems within it like the high level of foreign control. These structural problems should not simply be masked with high interest rates. The Conservatives should not be making it harder for Canadian business and agriculture not only to expand, but simply to operate, because of these high interest rates. The government's high interest rate policy is having an adverse effect on the entire economy.
This impact is especially severe for small businesses which are primarily Canadian-controlled and which rely mainly on

borrowing from banks to operate. The Globe and Mail reported on October 15 that "more bankruptcies will be the end result of the Bank of Canada's recent epidemic interest rate increases". It quoted Paul Jerabec, vice-president of Dun-woody & Company, who said, "All sizes of business will be susceptible-small, medium and large".
Last December 13, 1978, the current President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens), while speaking on behalf of the Conservative party, said "that for every one half point interest rates go up, it costs business $375 million". This means that the Conservative high interest rate policy has already cost Canadians over $2 billion. John Bullock, the President of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, a leading spokesman for small business, has expressed fear that a downturn of consumer spending because of this high rate policy will leave small retailers with larger inventories of unsold goods, thereby increasing the number of business bankruptcies. Nothing has been done by this government about the hardships that will be created by these policies for Canadian small businesses and their employees.
The effects of the Conservatives' high interest rate policy are also damaging to farmers, especially beef producers. They also rely on bank financing in order to operate. High interest costs for them mean higher food costs. Peter Hannam, president of the Ontario Federation of Agriculture, is reported in an article which appeared in the Toronto Star on October 10 as saying that the mood of Ontario farmers "is turning to near outrage" at the high interest rates they must pay on loans for land, buildings and machinery. He is also reported as saying that the decision to fight inflation by raising interest rates "is ironic because in the food industry it is just feeding inflation."
These high interest rates are also bringing the housing and construction industry to a halt, with a potential loss of thousands of jobs in that sector alone.
I have in my hand the latest issue of Focus, the publication of the Housing and Urban Development Association of Canada. It quotes its president, Keith Paddick, as saying in a telegram to the Prime Minister:
we must also express our concern with the increases in prime lending rates and their effect on the residential construction industry and on the cost of doing business in general.
That publication goes on to state that he pointed out that "the high interest rates were discouraging initiation of new construction programs with the resultant loss of employment." Because of these high interest rates, Mr. Speaker, many people will not be able to afford new housing or to refinance existing housing. Any benefit that people might have expected from the new Conservative mortgage interest and property tax credit plan will be cancelled by this Conservative high interest rate policy.
The Conservatives did not promote the first version of this plan as a way of helping people to bear some of the burden of future high interest rates; instead, they said that people would be better off than they were before the plan and before the
November 6, 1979

election-that they would spend less money than they had been spending on mortgage interest and property tax payments. This will not be the case now. Instead, people will be back where they were before the Conservatives began raising interest rates. Many will obviously be worse off. It will cost many Canadians more for mortgages, even after the tax credit plan is in effect.
It is clear, Mr. Speaker, that the Conservatives' high interest rate policy has already adversely affected the economy. These effects will be even more clear as we move into the winter months. This is confirmed by the economic analysis done by the Department of Finance. I persuaded-perhaps forced-the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) to table this document before the finance committee when he appeared there a few days ago. In the document, the effects of this Conservative policy are laid out clearly for all to see. It was prepared by the minister's own advisers within the Department of Finance.
The Conservatives now say that they cannot keep their economic promises and that they cannot do anything because the economy is in such bad shape. I say this is not accurate, or at least it was not accurate when they took office five months ago.

speechtext:
Not only was the economy in better shape then, than it had been for a long time previously-of course there was still room for improvement-but both the cost of living was lower and the rate of unemployment was lower than they had been for some time. If the Conservatives thought the economy was in such bad shape, they certainly have not proven it by their actions since becoming the government. They have allowed the economic policies of the previous Liberal government to continue almost unchanged in the almost half a year since they took office. What an endorsement that is! What a contradiction of their election arguments and their present claims about what Liberal policies have done to the economy!
They could have called Parliament sooner and had a budget four months ago, but instead, all we have seen is the support and encouragement by the Conservatives of a policy of moving interest rates in Canada to record levels-above 14 per cent. Before the election the Conservatives pledged that if they formed the government they would bring interest rates down.
The New Democratic Party has been showing a great deal of worry about the Liberal party's position on interest rates. Perhaps it is because when the Liberals are, in fact, liberal in policy orientation and action, the NDP is condemned to remain forever what they are now-the party of the radical nowhere.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-SEVERE ECONOMIC HARDSHIP FOR CANADIANS
speechtext:
The public can see through the sanctimonious pose and the self-righteousness of the NDP, and realize they have no valid claim to any special concern for the problems of average Canadians and their families. These are the concerns
Severe Economic Hardship
of the Liberals, Mr. Speaker, and this is demonstrated by the position taken in this motion of non-confidence.
For some members on this side, Mr. Speaker, there may well have been an argument for allowing interest rates to rise a year ago when it still meant they were only one or two points above the level of inflation, but when the Conservatives allowed our interest rates to go above 14 per cent, five points higher than the rate of inflation, then I think it is a different matter. It means a frontier has been crossed into dangerous, uncharted territory for the Canadian economy. As a result, I believe it is right and necessary for Liberals to take a new approach and a new look at interest rate policy.
But most important, it was the Conservatives who said, before the election, that if they formed the government they would bring interest rates down. That is what the Prime Minister said when he was leader of the opposition. The Conservatives did not say they would do this only after allowing interest rates to rise more and more until they reached record levels. They did not say they would do it only after the economy was better, so how can they say now that they cannot act because, they claim, the economy is worse than they expected?
Last July the Minister of Finance admitted that the economy was better than ever the Liberals had said it was going to be. In any event, the Conservatives have not shown that they have found any significant new information that was not available to them before the election about the state of the economy.
They promised low interest rates and a lot of other things at a time when they were saying that the economy was a lot worse than, in fact, it has turned out to be. They are the government now, they have the power to act, and they are doing nothing except allowing interest rates to rise.
When they eventually bring down a budget, if there is anything useful in it, it will likely be too late to help the economy. It takes six months for measures designed to help create jobs and increase production to work their way through the economy and have a beneficial effect.
I will continue, therefore, Mr. Speaker, to speak out, and Liberals will be speaking out and calling for policies like the implementation of an industrial strategy, a program involving co-operation between business and labour, but requiring something that we have not had up till now, and that we will not get, and that is federal government leadership to make sure that our economy is more productive and efficient. This means a policy to deal with problems like our balance of payments situation and the high level of foreign control of our economy. It means a policy which makes it possible for Canadian industry to meet more of our needs in Canada and to sell more abroad in competitive world markets. I am talking about jobs, and progress for millions of Canadians and their families, Mr. Speaker. That is something that the Conservatives and the NDP are not capable of providing.
The case for this motion when it deals with interest rates was made even before it was tabled, by leading members of the

November 6, 1979
Severe Economic Hardship
Conservatives such as the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), and the hon. member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan). The case was made well before the Conservatives even took office and began the series of increases in interest rates which has brought them to their present record levels.
As I have already pointed out, on March 2, when the Prime Minister was speaking as leader of the Progressive Conservative Party, he said that "high interest rates block growth and there is no proof that they stabilize the dollar." He also said that "they put in question major construction projects, by adding significantly to their capital costs and hit particularly hard at small businessmen who do not have the market power to pass along high money costs." At that time the Prime Minister also said that "interest rates must come down if we are to get the Canadian economy growing at its full potential." He promised that "it would be the policy of a Progressive Conservative government to gradually bring those interest rates down."
So, Mr. Speaker, when the Conservatives ask for alternatives to their present high interest rate policy, I want to tell them that one alternative, which has not been rebutted, would be to implement their own original policy as stated by the Prime Minister-"bring those interest rates down." The Liberals and I generally want action taken now to prevent the hardship this Conservative high interest rate policy is creating for millions of Canadians and their families.

November 6, 1979
Mr. Fabien Roy, M.P. Room 358 Centre Block House of Commons Parliament Buildings Ottawa, Ontario K1A0A6
Dear Mr. Roy:
This is in response to your letter to me of November 5, expressing concerns about oil supply for the coming winter, particularly in the eastern part of our country.
When the government came to power, we found that the situation regarding oil supply and pricing was out of control. Necessary long-term measures to assure an adequate and secure supply of oil for Canadian consumers had not been taken. The country is now paying for the previous government's lack of foresight and as a result faces a period of probably growing import dependence. As you know, we are now working vigorously to reverse this situation and to put in place policies which will achieve national oil self-sufficiency by 1990.
The short-term situation as we found it last June was also far from satisfactory. Inventories had been seriously depleted and there was considerable uncertainty about the adequacy of gasoline supply for the summer and heating oil for the winter.
The government acted promptly to improve the situation and to secure equitable treatment for the independent sector of the business. Thus:
1.	With the co-operation of the government of Alberta and its agencies, production of crude oil in western Canada has been brought to maximum levels in recent months.
2.	Exports of our valuable light crude oil were reduced from 55,000 barrels a day in September to 14,000 barrels a day in October and virtually eliminated in November in order to make this oil available to Canadian refiners.
3.	With the government's approval, the National Energy Board has continued to allow the exchange of western Canadian oil for additional supplies of overseas oil to eastern Canada. The Energy Board recently approved exchanges
totalling some 2.5 million barrels, virtually all of which are for the account of refiners in the province of Quebec.
4.	The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has authorized the payment of special import compensation in the amount of $745,000 to enable a Quebec refiner to import a badly-needed cargo of crude oil despite an unexpected increase in its price.
5.	On July 13 the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources released a report of an inquiry into problems which distributors, particularly in Quebec had faced last winter. The recommendations of the inquiry are being vigorously pursued.
6.	On August 15 the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources telexed the refiners regarding the question of supply for the independent sector of the business. He referred to exchanges being used as a means to assure supply to the independents. You can assume that this was a consideration in the National Energy Board's decision to make exchange oil available to certain refiners under item 3 above.
7.	Full use has been made of the capacity of the Interprovincial Pipe Line Limited, the carrier of crude oil from western Canada, to deliver oil to Quebec.
8.	In response to a National Energy Board request, Interprovincial made certain changes to its regulations in October with a view to avoiding discrimination against companies which have no history of shipment through the pipeline. As a result of these changes, a group of Quebec heating oil distributors will receive about 450,000 barrels of crude oil directly from western Canada in the month of November for processing into the oil products they need.
9.	Finally, my staff have kept continuously in touch with officials of provincial governments, the oil refiners and independent distributors regarding oil supply. These consultations have contributed to a better understanding all round. The number of resellers facing supply problems has sharply diminished.
Should we be faced with a disruption of oil supply sufficient to cause a national emergency, then I can assure you that the government is prepared to use the powers available to it under the Energy Supplies Emergency Act, 1979, to conserve supplies and to provide for their equitable distribution.
In this connection, you may have noted that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has indicated his intention to seek some administrative changes to the Energy Supplies
November 6, 1979

Emergency Act and at the same time announce appointment of an Energy Supplies Allocation Board. Part of this board's duties under the act is to ensure that Canada is fully prepared to meet any petroleum supply emergency with well-prepared and timely plans for action. Emergency planning has been proceeding in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources for some time and the level of this activity has been stepped up this year, with co-operation from private industry and the provinces.
While emergency planning is an essential and ongoing activity, I believe that the efforts of the private oil industry together with the government measures I have outlined will result in sufficient oil supplies being available for the coming winter. This assumes of course that there will be no major disruptions
in oil imports or in the operations of our own oil industry. In this general connection, I would draw your attention to the National Energy Board's statement of November 2 regarding short-term oil supplies, a copy of which is attached.
In conclusion, I can assure you that the government attaches the highest priority to the development of policies and programs which will assure oil supplies for Canadian consumers now and in the longer term. We are determined to overcome the oil supply problems left with us and the Canadian people by the previous government.
Yours sincerely, Joe Clark
